Keywords:                                                 Ship transport of liquefied carbon dioxide (LCO2) is competitive for long-distance transportation in the supply
Liquified CO2 transportation                              chain of carbon capture and storage, but inevitably has a problem of pressurization due to boil-off gas (BOG)
Boil-off gas                                              generation from the low-temperature LCO2. Conventionally, BOG can be vented, but it results in increased
Cargo handling system
                                                          greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This study suggests two advanced cargo handling systems (CHS) of continu­
Re-liquefaction system
Thermodynamic analysis
                                                          ously and periodically operated re-liquefaction for handling the LCO2 BOG, and compares the GHG intensity with
Greenhouse gas intensity                                  that of the BOG venting case. A new index of marine transportation GHG intensity (MGI) was developed to
                                                          accurately evaluate the well-to-wake GHG intensity of shipping and advanced CHS. An integrated model of the
                                                          tank and CHS was built to evaluate their continuous interaction. The results with BOR0 (design specification of
                                                          boil-off rate) of 0.15 % show that the venting case has a lower MGI up to 13 days of short voyage, but the re-
                                                          liquefaction systems are preferable for longer voyages because vented CO2 increases faster in the venting
                                                          case. Additionally, the periodically operated re-liquefaction system can be considerable for a wide range of
                                                          voyage days, as it enables flexible operation to cover shorter voyages with low BOR0.

     As shown in Fig. 6, a simulation model is built to estimate thermo­
dynamic tank behavior. The properties of the vapor, interface, liquid,
filling ratio, and f factor of the tank are obtained based on the initial
conditions of initial pressure (P0), filling ratio (FR0), heat entering
through the wall (Qtot), and tank geometry (Vtank and (L/D)tank). The
interface and surface areas of the vapor and liquid were determined
based on the tank geometry and filling ratio. The heat entering the vapor
and liquid and the heat exchanged at the interface can be calculated
using these values. Subsequently, the property change after heat is
injected is estimated, and the pressure that makes the volume of the
vapor and liquid equal to the tank volume is determined. This process is
repeated until the end of the voyage. The thermal properties of CO2 are
estimated using the Peng–Robinson EOS in Aspen HYSYS v14, and the
